Did Canada Just Sign Its Own Economic Death Warrant?

Canadian Prime Minister and WEF globalist Mark Carney has been a disaster for Canada since he entered office.  There were many critics who believed the Trudeau regime could not be topped in terms of self destructive behavior, but one could easily argue that Carney is far more dangerous and far more devious.

This week the Canadian government abandoned a nearly finalized trade deal with the US in the final hour of talks, leaving many analysts (and Canadians) bewildered.  According to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and related reports on the negotiations, the U.S. offered significant tariff reductions that would have given Canada preferential treatment relative to other major exporters.  

The offer included a reduction of tariffs on steel from 50% to 25%, a reduction on Canadian autos from 25% to 15%, a removal of the 10% tariff on Canadian lumber and cooperation on numerous other measures, representing the best deal offered in comparison to any other country which relies on heavily US markets.  Carney abruptly ordered negotiators to walk away, claiming the deal was "not good enough", and declared further retaliation against the US.  

So basically, Carney is saying:
Canadians will lose buying power, pay more for goods, and lose jobs, but it’s a sacrifice I’m willing to make to save face with the “elbows up” crowd. pic.twitter.com/cGVMnahbxy

— Pascal Anglehart (@DemosKratosCA) August 22, 2026

As of this moment 50% tariffs have been implemented on the majority of Canadian goods - The sudden shift represents economic suicide for Canada given their deep dependence on the US.  And what Carney doesn't tell Canadian citizens is, there are no practical alternatives to fill the trade void left behind.

Around 78% of all Canadian exports rely on US consumer markets.  These goods and resources only make up around 13% of all US imports.  Meanwhile, around 15% of US exports go to Canada.  In the US, exports make up 11% of total GDP.  In Canada, exports make up 33% of GDP.  

Economic is partially about psychology, but it's mostly about numbers, and the numbers just don't add up for the "Great White North".  By every metric, Canada needs the US more than the US need Canada.  Without these exports, Canada would suffer severe instability within a few years.    

The Canadian Central Bank, though, has tried to dismiss the dangers of prolonged trade disruptions with the US and Carney has sought to temper public concerns with posturing and bluster:

He will burn us to the ground for Quebec. pic.twitter.com/2OaPPhplSO

Carney has been pursuing trade deals with the EU and China in an attempt to "replace" US markets and save Canadian exports.  These agreements are being hailed by the Davos crowd as a "New World Order" that decouples from the US economy.  However, there are a number of problems.

In other words, Carney claims to be saving Canada from being dominated by the US, but he will end up selling his nation's sovereignty to China or the EU just to spite the Trump Administration.

Carney's behavior in light of these negotiations might seem bizarre, but it makes perfect sense if we consider the possibility that his goal is to cripple the Canadian economy deliberately and make it a pawn in a greater war waged by the Davos elite to isolate conservative movements in the US.  The majority of anti-globalist and anti-multicultural movements around the world rely on American efforts to defeat the progressive agenda.

Tehran At The Crossroads: Iran's Civilian Leaders Call For Peace Amid Crippling U.S. Blockade

Iran's top civilian officials are publicly urging an end to the ongoing conflict with the United States, exposing a deepening internal rift as they attempt to rein in hardliners who champion continued resistance.

The financial and social toll of the U.S. blockade is proving too severe to ignore - as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian recently declared that the country cannot endure a state of perpetual limbo, though he cautioned against making concessions that would appear humiliating on the global stage.

"The war must come to an end at some point," Pezeshkian stated in a Friday address, according to state media. "It is better that we demonstrate our strength and dignity today and tell the world that we have won and that we are ending the war."

President Donald Trump has maintained a relentless blockade on the Islamic Republic after a previous memorandum of understanding imploded - effectively severing the regime's ability to export oil - its primary source of income. This has plunged Iran into a domestic crisis characterized by skyrocketing inflation and an increasingly desperate cost-of-living crisis. The pressure is expected to intensify further this week, as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent prepares to unveil what President Trump has characterized as an "economic D-Day."

While the exact nature of these punitive measures remains classified, Bessent has strongly signaled the implementation of sweeping secondary sanctions targeting any nation that continues to do business with Tehran.

A Regime Divided

The push for diplomacy from Iran's civilian government stands in stark contrast to the shifting power dynamics among its clerics and military elite. Pezeshkian claims his diplomatic push aligns with the broader goals of the regime, referencing past speeches by Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei - who has conspicuously vanished from the public eye since the conflict escalated.

"I was in the presence of the Supreme Leader, and in his speeches as well, he openly stated that we must move beyond this state of 'neither war nor peace,'" Pezeshkian noted. "We are not going to humiliatingly back down before the enemy or bow our heads. We can sit down with strength, but also with logic, and resolve our problems."

Prior to his public absence, Khamenei had elevated hardline factions who favor military confrontation over the moderates seeking a renewed deal with Washington. Despite this, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf echoed the President's warnings, underscoring the severe national security risks of a collapsing economy.

"No matter how much military power we have, if our people are struggling and the country lacks financial circulation and economic growth, we will not achieve progress," Ghalibaf stated. "As someone who has experienced war, I understand the true value of peace."

Washington's Stance: The "Right Deal"

The Trump administration's distrust stems from the fraught history of recent negotiations, during which U.S. officials reported receiving deeply conflicting signals from Tehran. The previous agreement shattered after Iran launched a series of strikes on maritime vessels navigating the Strait of Hormuz.

For the United States, the objectives remain twofold and uncompromising: Nuclear Prevention: Ensuring Iran permanently loses the capacity to develop or acquire a nuclear weapon. Maritime Security: The full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to global trade.

Currently, the Trump administration claims it's securing the safe passage of 8 to 9 million barrels of oil through the strait daily - a steep decline from the roughly 20 million barrels that traversed the waterway before the conflict erupted.

Washington is signaling that it will dictate the terms. Addressing reporters on Friday, President Trump summarized the diplomatic standoff: "They would love to make a deal, but they're not ready to make the right deal."

items.title: Azerbaijan Sues CNN Over Story On Cooperation With Israel In War On Iran
items.content_text:
Azerbaijan Sues CNN Over Story On Cooperation With Israel In War On Iran

Authored by Jonathan Turley,

There is a novel (and highly dubious) lawsuit filed in Delaware by the nation of Azerbaijan against CNN for a story claiming that it was cooperating with Israel in attacks on Iran. Republic of Azerbaijan v. CNN, Inc. borders on the legally frivolous, but it is likely politically advantageous to show Iran that it contests the allegations.

In its Complaint, Azerbaijan details the development of hostilities while maintaining neutrality:

Azerbaijan, which shares a border with Iran to the south, is not and has never been a participant in the Iran War. Azerbaijan has not supported military operations by any of the warring nations.

...Azerbaijan maintains a policy of neutrality and independence. Azerbaijan does not host any foreign military bases on its territory and, as a non-aligned state, maintains a strict official policy and legislative framework against foreign military footprints.

The basis for the lawsuit is what the country calls "CNN's reckless reporting" on June 5, 2026 in a post titled "Exclusive: Israel sent troops to Azerbaijan during Iran war, sources say." The article claiming that Azerbaijan allowed Israel to use its territory to launch attacks against Iran no doubt raised the ire of the Islamic Republic.

Indeed, the Complaint lays out how Iran threatened any countries assisting Iran and suggested that the story was putting them at risk of an Iranian attack:

Ali Larijani, a senior Iranian official, threatened: 'The countries of the region must either prevent the use of their soil by America against Iran themselves, or we will.' Similarly, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps ("IRGC") has issued a press release unambiguously stating that 'Countries that host the aggressor American military and have placed their land at the disposal of the aggressor criminals for attacks on Iran should be prepared to receive a corresponding response, and should activate their civil defence [sic] units to safeguard the lives of their citizens and move them away from likely targets.'

The complaint, however, faces even more daunting legal challenges. While the Complaint alleges that "CNN's false reporting caused reputational harm to Azerbaijan and threatens tenuous international relations," it is doubtful that a court will view this as a viable tort claim under defamation.

We have previously discussed lawsuits by countries or nationality groups that have been dismissed. The leading case on defamation, New York Times v. Sullivan, expressly states, "For good reason, "no court of last resort in this country has ever held, or even suggested, that prosecutions for libel on government have any place in the American system of jurisprudence."

In 2000, a state court dismissed Air Zimbabwe v. Chicago Tribune Co. (Cal. Super. Ct. 2000), due to the fact that Air Zimbabwe is "a government entity, is precluded under the First Amendment from pursuing a defamation claim."

Moreover, there are elemental problems in making such a claim. A country would be treated as a public official or figure subject to the "actual malice" standard, requiring knowing falsehood or reckless disregard of the truth. CNN clearly had sources that led it to believe the accounts were true. Indeed, many countries, including those asserting neutrality, have secret agreements or accommodations in this and other wars.

Proving that no such agreement existed or that there was not a defensible basis for the story would be very difficult.

The question of harm is also intriguing. Many would view cooperating against Iran as an admirable decision for Azerbaijan. Although it clearly puts Azerbaijan at odds with Iran, it puts it in alignment with other countries such as the United States. It is difficult to see how damages would be measured in such a circumstance, even if a viable claim on the merits could be established.

This case asks a court to adjudicate global political questions with shadowy sources and factual claims. I would be surprised if any court would relish such a trial and expect that Republic of Azerbaijan v. CNN, Inc. will soon join the list of dismissed actions.

items.title: Valve 诞生 30 周年
items.content_text: Valve 由前微软员工 Gabe Newell 和 Mike Harrington 创办于 1996 年 8 月 24 日，该公司的第一款游戏是备受好评的《半条命》，它被认为对 FPS 这一游戏类别产生了深远影响。Harrington 于 2000 年离开 Valve。Valve 在 2003 年开发了 Steam，之后随《半条命2》的发布强制捆绑推送给玩家，此举曾引起广泛批评，但它最终成为 Valve 最主要的收入来源，它过于成功以至于部分导致 Valve 大幅减少了游戏新作的开发速度。Valve 的游戏开发主要集中在 2013 年前，它发布了一系列享有盛誉的游戏作品，包括《反恐精英》系列、《传送门》系列，《求生之路》系列和《Dota 2》。2020 年代之后的新作包括 VR 游戏《Half-Life: Alyx》，以及仍然在封闭测试的多人游戏《Deadlock》。Valve 还开发了一系列硬件产品，包括 Linux 游戏机 Steam Machine、掌机 Steam Deck 和 VR 头显 Valve Index。

items.title: 国际计量大会将讨论用闰时取代闰秒
items.content_text: 今年 10 月在法国举行的国际计量大会将讨论用闰时取代闰秒。闰秒需要经常性修改，会导致混乱，而引入闰时后数百年内无需修改。协调世界时（UTC）基于用原子振动实现的高精度原子钟来确定，成为 1 秒长度的标准。不过由地球自转时间决定的 1 天长度会发生不规则变化，因此会产生偏差。地球的自转速度根据潮汐涨落以及地球内部地核运动而波动。地球的一天即地球自转一圈，大约需要 86,400 秒。闰秒的作用就是调整与原子钟的偏差，当偏差累积即将超过 0.9 秒时，就会在一天中增加1秒。1972 年引入闰秒以来已修改了 27 次。然而对于需要同步时间进行自动控制的金融交易、交通、电力等高端通信系统而言，哪怕是微小的误差也可能导致整个网络陷入混乱。2012 年增加闰秒时大型网络服务等发生故障。因此美国 IT 巨头 Google 和微软等方面为避免影响而引入各自的调整方法。各公司采用的“时间系统”各不相同，导致闰秒作为标准时间基准的地位动摇。

items.content_text: TikTok 与字节跳动同意支付 4 亿美元与美国司法部就儿童网络隐私争议达成和解。美国司法部 2024 年代表联邦贸易委员会（FTC）起诉 TikTok，指控 TikTok 允许数百万名 13 岁以下儿童在家长不知情或未同意的情况下创建账户，并设置障碍，让家长难以要求删除这些账户。诉讼指 TikTok 违反儿童网络隐私法，在未取得家长同意的情况下收集儿童个人资料。TikTok 与字节跳动同意达成一项 4 亿美元的和解协议，以解决美国司法部对 TikTok 的指控。

items.title: 嫦娥七号推迟到明年发射
items.content_text: 中国载人航天工程网周日发表一句话声明：“本着稳妥可靠、万无一失的原则，经综合研判，嫦娥七号任务不满足发射条件，不能在今年预定窗口实施。”官方没有解释原因。嫦娥七号原计划的发射窗口是 2026 年 8 月 24 日上午。下一个发射窗口可能是明年 2 月或 3 月。推迟发射的一个可能原因是台风娜拉的影响，娜拉正在海南文昌发射场附近海域徘徊，在发射窗口关闭前，天气状况不太可能好转。嫦娥七号将登陆月球南极，寻找水冰，探测器对登陆地区的日照条件要求较高。

items.title: 摩托罗拉的 GrapheneOS 手机预计比 Pixel 手机更贵
items.content_text: 摩托罗拉正与 Android 安全加固项目 GrapheneOS 合作，准备在 2027 年推出支持 GrapheneOS 的智能手机。GrapheneOS 目前只支持 Google 的 Pixel 智能手机，原因是 Pixel 使用的 Tensor SoC 提供了项目所需的安全特性，但不是所有高通手机芯片都提供了类似的安全特性。高通只有最昂贵的 8 系列芯片才具有类似安全功能。这意味着摩托罗拉只有高端旗舰型号才能支持 GrapheneOS，而此类型号价格不菲。GrapheneOS 项目透露其定价甚至比 Pixel 手机更贵。最新的 Pixel 11 系列起售价为 900 美元。 摩托罗拉未来的中低端型号可能会支持 GrapheneOS，但在短时间内不会发生。

items.title: 九成生物医学论文有 AI 辅助写作痕迹
items.content_text: 在论文写作中使用 AI 的情况可能比以前认为的更普遍。根据发表在 arXiv 上的一篇预印本，对 PubMed Central 数据库收录的 2025 年全年发表的英文论文的分析显示，LLM 的使用比例高达 77%，而 2024 年这一比例为 52%。这一结论与 2025 年进行的一项调查结果一致。调查显示，71% 的研究人员表示在使用 AI 辅助写作——实际使用率可能高于承认的水平。2025 年 12 月发表的论文有近九成出现了 AI 辅助写作的痕迹。最新研究还发现，AI 辅助写作在摘要、引言和讨论部分比在方法和结果部分更为常见。

items.title: 调查显示三分之一英文网页有 AI 创作痕迹
items.content_text: 美国皮尤研究中心的数据科学家使用 AI 检测工具分析了过去五年的 50 万英文网页，估计其中 AI 撰写内容的比例。所有这些样本网页中，十分之一有明显 AI 创作痕迹。在 OpenAI 的 AI 工具 ChatGPT 于 2022 年底推出之后，AI 内容的比例在不断上升。2026 年 7 月的快照中，逾三分之一 ChatGPT 推出后发布的网页显示出 AI 创作的痕迹。在主要顶级域名中 AI 创作文本的分布并不均匀。ChatGPT 最初发布时 AI 语言模式在 .com、.org、.edu 和 .gov 等域名上的出现频率大致相同。但 2026 年的样本中十分之一的 .com 域名显示出 AI 创作的痕迹，是 .org 域名（4.6%）的两倍，.edu 或.gov域名（1%）的十倍。相比 2023 年，今天的网页：破折号的使用频率增加了一倍；牛津逗号的使用频率增加了 63%；AI 常用词如 delve、interplay 或 testament 的使用频率增加了一倍以上；it's not just X, it's Y 的负面/对比平行语言模式几乎是之前的三倍。

items.title: 免费游戏隐藏的高成本
items.content_text: 免费游戏并不真免费，游戏内虚拟物品的售价可能比一款典型 3A 游戏的定价高得多。免费游戏内的虚拟交易通常被称为微交易，然而很多微交易动辄上百美元，“微”之名其实名不副实。根据《Frontiers in Public Health》上的一项研究，研究人员基于 2308 名 10-19 岁奥地利学生（48.8% 为男性；平均年龄 14.3 岁）的数据，分析了游戏内消费的分布情况及其与游戏成瘾、赌博成瘾和社会经济地位的关联。他们发现，支出前 10% 的青少年贡献了 61.4% 的总消费额；重度消费者比轻度消费者更容易出现游戏成瘾和赌博成瘾；高消费额并非仅限于家庭经济条件较好的青少年。研究人员认为，免费游戏这种消费模式与赌博行业高度相似，但相比高度监管的赌博行业，游戏行业受到的监管要少得多。他们呼吁为保护青少年加强监管。

items.title: 极端磁场改变光传播方式
items.content_text: 天文学家首次利用天然极端磁场，即对磁星信号的观测研究，为 90 年前德国物理学家海森堡作出的量子电动力学预言提供了迄今最有力的证据：看似空无一物的真空，在极端磁场中会改变光的传播方式，产生真空双折射效应。研究人员利用 NASA 成像 X射 线偏振探测器，对编号 1E 1547.0-5408 的射电磁星进行了观测，并结合国际空间站 X 射线望远镜以及澳大利亚帕克斯射电望远镜的数据展开分析。磁星是大质量恒星爆炸后留下的致密残骸，拥有宇宙已知最强的磁场。理论认为，当磁场足够强时，真空不再是无性质的虚空，而是表现出类似晶体的光学性质，使不同偏振方向的光以不同速度传播，从而改变 X 射线偏振特征。1E1547.0-5408 每两秒自转一周，是少数能持续发射射电波的磁星之一。2025 年 3 月和 4 月，团队将探测器指向这颗天体。结果显示，其 X 射线偏振度接近同类天体的 3倍，且偏振方向与恒星磁场方向完全一致，这一特征符合海森堡等人预测的真空双折射效应。

items.title: 机器人短跑超越人类，但刹住是问题
items.content_text: 为期五天的世界人形机器人运动会于周六在北京开幕。运动会共设 51 个项目，包括 30 项体育竞技和 21 项场景化竞赛。超过 40% 的项目要求机器人完全自主运行。在 8 月 22 日的首日赛事中，两台机器人跑出了比人类百米世界纪录(9.58秒)保持者博尔特(Usain Bolt)更快的成绩，相比去年百米短跑仍然耗时 20 秒以上的机器人，可谓进步巨大。另一台机器人则在 400 米短跑中实现了 39.7 秒的成绩，超越了南非运动员 Wayde van Niekerk 43.03 秒的世界纪录。不过，在冲过终点线后，这些机器人的制动能力依然存在很大缺陷。现场画面显示，机器人纷纷撞向十几米开外的巨大软垫，然后跌倒在地，多台机器人翻倒后甚至出现了明显损坏。这次运动会还设置了在模拟工厂、餐厅、办公室及紧急情况场景下测试机器人性能的比赛项目。比如人形机器人能否在处理包装和仓储作业的同时，可靠地完成诸如线缆连接等精密任务？它们能否应对角度不当的线缆、刚好够不到的物体、发生位移的包裹等工厂中常见的困难？这些任务旨在评估它们在那些不那么引人注目的岗位上像人类一样工作的能力。

items.title: 卡巴斯基发现第一种针对汽车的 Android 恶意程序
items.content_text: 俄罗斯安全公司卡巴斯基的研究人员报告他们发现第一种针对汽车的 Android 恶意程序。恶意程序通过基于 Android 的兜风出行汽车主机（head unit）固件的内置更新程序传播，被认为与 MoYu Group 黑客组织有关，该组织与 BADBOX 僵尸网络有关联。卡巴斯基称它已经通知了兜风出行，对方表示已修复相关安全问题。这一汽车恶意程序传播案例类似廉价电视盒，攻击者旨在创建住宅代理僵尸网络，因此使用了相同的网络基础设施。

items.title: 柳树和杨树释放出的化合物会恶化城市空气质量
items.content_text: 数百万棵垂柳和白杨树将北京装缀成一个绿色的大都市。然而根据《Science Advances》上发表的一项研究，柳树和杨树释放出的化合物是城市空气污染的重要来源。广州暨南大学的研究人员最初想要了解人类活动对臭氧污染的影响，结果意外发现城市植被是臭氧的重要来源。植物会释放出挥发性有机化合物，作为植物光合作用的副产品，被广泛种植的柳树和杨树会释放出大量的异戊二烯。研究团队发现，北京 35% 的树木会释放异戊二烯。研究人员在北京各地采集空气样本，测量挥发性有机化合物浓度，在城市各监测站收集臭氧数据。研究发现，在 2021 年 5 月至 7 月期间，植物排放的化合物约占北京总排放量的 10%，其余来自人类活动如汽车尾气和工业化学品。植物释放出的挥发性有机化合物与大气中的羟基反应生成过氧自由基，过氧自由基再与空气中的氮氧化物（NOx）反应生成化合物，这些化合物在阳光照射下会转化为臭氧。研究发现，植物排放的有机化合物占最终生成臭氧的化学物质的 52%，其中异戊二烯是主要贡献者。人类活动产生的挥发性有机化合物总排放量高于植物排放，但对生成臭氧的贡献远小于植物。研究人员还调查了 24 个特大城市种植的树种，发现澳大利亚悉尼和墨尔本所种植树的异戊二烯排放量预计会高于北京，悉尼有 65% 的树木会排放异戊二烯。

items.title: 波兰加密货币交易所 CEO 在 2022 年失踪，4 年后他的继任者也失踪了
items.content_text: Nicole Suszek 最后一次收到哥哥 Sylwester 的电话语音留言是在 2022 年，在留言中 Sylwester 急迫的请求她给他寄去比特币，否则以后就永远见不到面了。Sylwester 从此杳无音信，家人认为他已经遇害。Sylwester 是东欧和中欧最大加密货币交易所 Zondacrypto 的创始人，他在 2014 年创办了 Zondacrypto 的前身 BitBay。接替 Sylwester 担任 Zondacrypto CEO 的波兰律师 Przemyslaw Kral 在今年四月也失踪了，这一事件让 Sylwester 案再次浮出水面。波兰总理 Donald Tusk 则指责 Zondacrypto 与俄罗斯情报机构、有组织犯罪和右 翼政客有关联。Zondacrypto 网站在 4 月关闭，导致数十万客户无法提现或交易。Zondacrypto 发行的代币 ZND 已贬值逾 99.9%。Przemyslaw Kral 最后一次露面是在 4 月 16 日，他通过社媒发表了一则视频，呼吁客户不要恐慌，不要对交易所失去信心，称公司还有 4000 比特币，但这些比特币所在的钱包密钥只有前 CEO 才知道。加密货币专家对此表示怀疑，因为该钱包已有近十年没有活动了。对于 Kral 身在何处，有人据称曾在以色列、博茨瓦纳和迪拜等地目击到他，但这些说法都未经证实。代表 Zondacrypto 账户被冻结客户的华沙律师 Robert Nogacki 认为  Kral 在东南亚，他表示关于 Zondacrypto 他唯一确定的就是：“它从一开始就是个骗局。”

items.title: 3 分钟冲刺跑产生的分子反应与 90 分钟中等强度运动截然不同
items.content_text: 3 分钟冲刺跑产生的分子反应与 90 分钟中等强度运动截然不同。洛克菲勒大学的研究人员比较了人体对不同强度运动的反应。他们发现，六次 30 秒全力冲刺跑后，血液中近四分之一的蛋白质发生了变化。相比之下，90 分钟持续中等强度骑行仅改变了不到 0.25% 的蛋白质。中等强度的跑步机运动对蛋白质的影响比骑行更大，但仍然远小于短暂的冲刺跑。冲刺跑还改变了逾 200 种代谢物，迅速提升了参与血管生长、组织重塑和激素信号传导的蛋白质水平。部分蛋白质是通过一种名为胞外域脱落（ectodomain shedding）的快速细胞信号传导过程进入血液的——蛋白质并非新产生并释放，而是细胞表面已有的蛋白质片段被切除并迅速进入血液循环。33 种与降低心血管和代谢疾病风险相关的蛋白质有 32 种会因短暂的冲刺跑发生改变，只有 3 种会受到中等强度运动的影响。逾四分之一蛋白质还与延缓生物衰老相关。研究结果表明，运动强度可能会强烈影响释放到血液中的蛋白质和代谢物，进而影响全身组织的反应方式。

items.title: Rockstar 向微软和 Discord 发去法庭传票以识别 GTA6 泄密者身份
items.content_text: 2022 年 9 月一名黑客泄漏了当时尚未宣布的 GTA6 的图片和视频，此事促使开发商 Rockstar Games 加强了安全措施。然而到了 2026 年 8 月游戏还有 3 个月即将发售时，自称 Cyber​​Leek 的个人或组织发布了 GTA6 的一系列新视频，视频显示泄密者手中可能有一个可运行的版本，也就是游戏本体被盗了。彭博社援引知情人士的消息称，Rockstar 尚未确定泄密者身份，也不知道游戏本体是如何泄漏出去的。该公司目前正全力查明泄露源头并追踪泄密者。为了识别泄密者，Rockstar 母公司 Take-Two 的律师正向法院申请传票，要求微软和 Discord 提供信息帮助识别泄密者身份。Take-Two 要求微软在 9 月 4 日前提供信息，要求 Discord 在相同的截止日期前提供 CYBERLEEK、CINEMATICROCKSTAR 和 Surfer24k™ 等账号的信息。

items.title: 因门把手安全隐患特斯拉在华召回近 300 万辆车
items.content_text: 特斯拉和另外 8 家汽车制造商 21 日宣布，将在中国召回总计约 430 万辆汽车，创下中国汽车召回规模纪录。此次召回的整改措施包括软件更新、加贴警示标签，以及改进门把手周围的标识等。大多数车企还将通过 OTA 远程升级软件。根据国家市场监督管理总局发布的公告，特斯拉将从 9 月 25 日起召回 298 万辆进口及中国制造的 Model 3、Model Y、Model S 和 Model X 汽车。特斯拉的召回规模最大，这也反映出该公司采用此类门把手设计的车型销量巨大。除特斯拉外，此次召回行动涉及车企包括中国一汽、北汽蓝谷、东风汽车、奇瑞、吉利、小鹏、零跑和小米。小米将召回约 39 万辆汽车，零跑约 37.1 万辆，小鹏约 26.4 万辆。零跑、小鹏和吉利此次召回的规模也均创下各自公司的历史纪录。监管机构表示，在发生严重碰撞并导致车辆电气系统失效后，机械式紧急车门解锁装置可能难以识别。车内人员可能难以打开车门逃生，救援人员也可能难以进入车内。

items.title: 使用胁迫密码删除手机数据的美国公民被控妨碍联邦执法的重罪
items.content_text: 2025 年 1 月，Samuel Tunick 从多米尼加共和国度假返回美国时，在亚特兰大 Hartsfield-Jackson 国际机场被拦下，美国海关和边境保护局官员要求搜查他的手机。他最终交出了手机以及一个密码，该密码删除了手机上的数据。他的 Pixel 智能手机运行的是安全加固的 Android 操作系统 GrapheneOS，它内置了被称为胁迫密码的安全功能，输入该密码后会删除手机上的数据。美国检方以妨碍联邦执法的重罪起诉了他，他因此面临最高五年的监禁。这是已知首个因输入特定密码删除设备数据而遭到起诉的案例。佐治亚州北区联邦检察官 Theodore Hertzberg 在一份声明中表示：“妨碍联邦执法是性质严重、有严重后果的罪行。任何销毁或试图销毁财产（包括数据）以阻止合法搜查和扣押的人，都应预料到会因其行为受到起诉和惩罚。”Tunick 在接受《纽约时报》采访时表示：“政府不拥有我们的数据。政府不拥有我们的通信、我们的人际关系，无论他们多么努力尝试。我们必须捍卫对隐私的基本权利；否则我们无法真正说自己生活在一个民主社会中。”

items.title: 中国要求政府部门提前停用 Windows 10 政府版改用 Linux
items.content_text: 彭博社报道，中国政府下令部分机构提前停止使用 Windows 10 中国政府版，改用国产 Linux 发行版。为维护数字主权，中国已不再信任美国公司的软件。微软回应彭博社的询问时表示它没有发现影响该 Windows 系统的安全事件。Windows 10 中国政府版由微软和中国电子科技集团的合资企业神州网信开发。神州网信原计划到 2027 年 2 月停止支持该版本，但其生命结束时间被提前到今年下半年。中国政府机构采用的国产 Linux 发行版可能包括了麒麟操作系统（Kylin OS)和统信 UOS。统信 UOS 桌面版源自 Deepin 和 Debian Linux。

items.title: 中国准备发射嫦娥七号，前往月球南极寻找水冰
items.content_text: 中国准备发射嫦娥七号，它将尝试首次直接在月球南极着陆，搜寻阴影区的陨石坑去寻找水冰。嫦娥七号使用的运载火箭为长征五号，计划从海南文昌航天发射场发射，发射窗口为 2026 年 8 月 24 日上午。嫦娥七号由一个轨道器和一个着陆器组成，而着陆器搭载了漫游的巡视器和飞跃器，其中飞跃器具备重复起飞着陆、月面飞行、月面行走功能。在阳照区完成探测并充电后，它将飞入有永久阴影区的撞击坑进行探测。嫦娥七号探测器将耗时时六天抵达月球轨道，随后将在轨道上展开为期两个月的准备工作，计划于 11 月着陆月球南极，预定着落地点为沙克尔顿撞击坑，它是一个直径 21 公里的环形山，边缘接近月球南极。月球两极被认为蕴藏了巨大的冰库，但其规模有多大、以及实际分布情况，都需要等待实地观察。

items.title: Transcript: Trump Seethes at Natalie Harp Mess as Leaks Grow Damning
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the August 24 episode of the Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

The furor around Donald Trump’s very devoted young aide, Natalie Harp, isn’t abating in the least, and new reporting indicates that anger inside the White House over this story—all driven by the fury of one person in particular—might have backfired, making the story even worse for him. This comes as new leaks also suggest Harp’s role is even more unnerving than we thought.

The whole saga indicates something important about Donald Trump’s political weakness right now, and how Dems can exploit it in today’s information environment. We’re talking about it all with Democratic strategist Greg Greene, who held the job of managing social media accounts under President Obama and wrote about this experience for The New Republic. Greg, good to have you on.

Greg Greene: Glad to be here.

Sargent: OK, so last week Senator Jon Ossoff pointed out that Trump doesn’t like doing the job as president, and instead likes to spend his time traveling with Natalie on the presidential plane. The White House and MAGA went absolutely haywire, resulting in a story that continues right now. Greg, can you bring us up to speed on all this?

Greene: Yes. Jon Ossoff really set off a furor by bringing Natalie into the conversation, and the story has spun out of control almost since then for the White House. What I would say is that I really got interested in this thinking about how Natalie Harp has access not only to the president himself, but also to his phone and to his social media accounts, which really raises questions, in my view, based on my experience, about the appropriateness of her role without supervision in the content that goes out.

Sargent: Yeah, and we’re going to get to that in a second. But we’re now getting new reporting from The Atlantic that reports that the White House freak-out over Harp was really a self-own. The White House publicly tried to humiliate journalists who wrote or asked about Harp, but that only persuaded more outlets that had ignored her role to write about her.

And then The Atlantic reports that aides inside the White House grew angrier because, according to sources, they were, quote, “taking their cues from a furious president.”

Greene: I agree with the White House staffers who believe that this approach to the conversation has really backfired on the White House. Natalie Harp is someone who people have covered since at least 2024.

Maggie Haberman has written about her role in the White House operation and the campaign operation before, but she managed to fly under the radar before now—when, thanks to the escapade in Ankara, Turkey, with the catering cart, she became a live wire in news coverage, in a heated story, and has been since then talked about in a way that really hasn’t served her interests or the president’s, in a time when the president’s approval ratings are already in the tank.

Sargent: Absolutely. And Greg, we know how Trump operates. It goes all the way back to Roy Cohn. It’s never concede error, always attack, always try to humiliate at all costs. What’s the difference between the way Natalie Harp and Trump are doing this versus the way you did it under Obama?

Greene: Well, the biggest difference is that there were many layers between myself and the president. As I say in the piece for The New Republic, I never wrote on a plane, never mind a catering cart. I spent my time at the Democratic National Committee working with colleagues there and consulting with the digital director, the communications director, and people inside the White House communications office to figure out what priorities we had for getting messages out, and to shape our posts around those agenda items.

So it was never an instance of one staffer—never mind myself—getting into the president’s ear and proposing material, because really it was an operation designed to support the presidency, rather than one person just whispering into another person’s ear.

Sargent: And you also didn’t decide what the president saw and what he doesn’t see. If the White House had said nothing, most reporters would have moved on very quickly. But then the vehemence of the reaction kind of stirs the interest of the reporters, because it starts to look like there’s some reason the White House doesn’t want this relationship with this young aide talked about. And boom, there’s the ingredient to really make it blow up.

You’ve been doing this stuff a long time. What does this tell us about how Washington works?

Greene: Well, I would say the first thing is that Washington loves a scandal. When I was at the University of Virginia as a student many, many years ago, I studied in a seminar with political scientist Larry Sabato about campaigns and elections. He wrote the book Feeding Frenzy, about how scandals develop and gain a momentum of their own. And what we’re seeing, perhaps for one of the first times in the Trump presidency, especially in his second term, is an example of that playing out in real life.

He has usually been able to escape this sort of cyclical scrutiny that amplifies as news cycles go on, one after the next. But this time people are really interested in Natalie Harp. And I have to say, they have reason to be, because the relationship between her and the president, and the fashion in which she manages the president’s communications—helping him text with world leaders, helping him craft his social media posts, his Truth Social—without having a gatekeeper in between her and the send button, is highly unusual.

Sargent: It sure is. Well, The New York Times talked to a bunch of advisors around Trump, and they were pretty happy to leak about Natalie Harp. They talked about how she’s really this information gatekeeper for Trump, and his advisors think that because of her, some of the information he gets is, quote, “poisonous and counterproductive,” as the Times put it.

And listen to this from the Times: “She supplies him with content she fishes out of the social media gutter, like the video he posted depicting the Obamas as apes.” Greg, I don’t get why that little nugget didn’t get more attention. It’s a big deal that she was behind him posting that, isn’t it?

Greene: It is a massive revelation. I was personally not shocked, but taken aback by that confirmation. And I would say that, just as a professional who’s been in the shoes of people who post to these accounts that are widely watched, there is a serious lack of editorial judgment that is spoken to by the idea of depicting any public figure in this country, especially a former president of the United States, as an ape. I don’t understand how that had not been a bigger story up to now.

Sargent: I mean, under a conventional presidency, something like that would be a firing offense. I get that Donald Trump has completely revamped the rules for everything and turned the whole idea of a firing offense and scandal into something completely different than it ever was before.

But I would think that if anything close to that happened under a Democratic president, and we knew from the pages of The New York Times that this particular aide fished out this image and got it put on social media under the president’s handle, you’d think that person would get fired instantly, wouldn’t you?

Greene: Yes, I absolutely do think someone would get fired instantly. And more than that, I can think of any number of people who you and I both know, from my time working at the Democratic National Committee, at whose hands I might not even be alive right now had I been so irresponsible with the privilege I had of administering those accounts. It is not only a firing offense, in my view, but it’s unspeakable.

Sargent: And so if she’s got this control over his social media feed—we’ve seen posts with him depicted as Jesus Christ and all these other types of posts that really deify him, that really go to the core of this kind of personalist-dictator vibe that he wants out there about himself. She’s clearly the key figure.

And you can kind of see something even more unnerving in all this, because we’ve now learned from reporting that she really deifies Donald Trump. And so from her letters and stuff like that, we’ve—she essentially dotes over him to the degree that she doesn’t want him to ever suffer any negative feelings of any kind. She wants to bring him joy and so forth and so on.

So you can kind of see where these posts depicting him as Jesus Christ are actually coming from. And I think that given that the whole world is seeing the American president depict himself as the Almighty, we want to know who’s behind that, I think.

Greene: Yes, absolutely. And there is a lack of perspective that is revealed in the letters that were reported yesterday in another publication, that she had written to the president—calling herself unworthy, asking for his approval and forgiveness. Things that I would never have contemplated doing, because, frankly, I was working for the betterment of the president and the presidency, and deliberately kept myself out of public view in my role writing that content, because my profile was not the point. The point was the president’s agenda, and the agenda of the people who helped to bring him to the White House.

Sargent: I think you really put your finger on an important distinction there, which is that under previous presidents—maybe somewhat less so under George W. Bush, but certainly under Democratic presidents—a lot of the senior staff that work with the president and shape his message and so forth understand the presidency as a public thing.

It’s not about one person. It’s about something that the country possesses. It’s an institution that is preserved from one administration to the next. It isn’t about the deification of one person. And under Donald Trump, tons have been written about how his presidency is functionally like a personalist one. But there you really see it very clearly.

The people around Trump do not see the presidency as a public thing, as something that he is stewarding and shepherding on behalf of the American people. They solely understand it as being only about him. And I think this story really reveals that very clearly. What do you think of that?

Greene: It’s really degrading and sordid to be governed in this way—to have the highest office in the land used as a vehicle for glorification of someone who would post material depicting a former president as an ape. Who would post material depicting himself as a fighter pilot dropping poop on No Kings protesters, who are his fellow Americans, on whose behalf he’s supposed to be governing.

It is a day-in and day-out sordid spectacle. And for me personally, I find this—I don’t take it as a personal embarrassment, because I’m not in the White House, I have long since been away from the role of posting social media for people in high office. But I do find this incredibly disappointing and concerning, because the access that she has, both to his information flow and to his accounts, really creates problems for people who are concerned about misuse of that access for various purposes, whether insider trading or worse.

Sargent: And we haven’t even probed yet—no reporters have really gotten to the core of whether she’s instrumental in his tweets that seem to undermine his own negotiators with Iran, for instance.

Greene: Exactly.

Sargent: There’s a paradox at the core of this I want to try to identify as well. Trump and MAGA really think that they have this boundless power to humiliate anyone who dares to criticize them, or really anyone who dares to tell the truth about them. They have this limitless ability to control the information space, they think. And so to them, they can just simply demolish anyone who talks about Harp and leave them in kind of smoking ruins or whatever.

But the problem for them is that the Natalie Harp story does reveal highly unnerving truths about this man’s temperament and total unfitness to be president. And once the story gets onto that topic, their power shrivels and disappears. That’s what we’re seeing here. What do you think of all that, Greg?

Greene: Yes, I do think their power to control and dictate the agenda does dissipate in moments like this. And what we’re seeing here with Natalie Harp is a picture of a White House run poorly, of a president with no self-restraint, with terrible instincts about what’s in the best interest of the country to publish.

And it’s being displayed in a visceral way, because we have also seen Natalie Harp being rescued from what the president considered to be an Air Force One at possible risk—over the head of the secretary of state and other Cabinet officers who are in the presidential line of succession. It is an incredible story about judgment and misjudgment, and it almost tells itself, but I’m glad to help tell part of it.

Sargent: Well, you certainly did. And one last thought on all this, to close. I think a lot of people, you know, in the media look at this and they say, OK, well, did Jon Ossoff err by, you know, making this personal? Did Jon Ossoff make a mistake by attacking a professional woman? Did Jon Ossoff open himself to attacks from the White House by appearing to insinuate things about Trump’s sexual habits or whatever?

And I just think that mindset that looks at it that way is wrong. And it’s actually an insider-D.C. mindset that just misses what I think you got at earlier, which is the degree to which this kind of stuff—seeing this president do this—is just degrading and terrible for us all to live under.

And I think the American people look at a story like this and they see it the way we’re describing it, not the way those D.C. insider types describe it. They see a story of someone who’s just wiping his ass with a public thing, which is the presidency. And they hate that. They hate the ballroom, they hate the Reflecting Pool nonsense.

I think this stuff really works against Trump and Republicans, and underscores that the Republican Party has just let this madman run amok with our stuff, right? And I think that’s the way the story is perceived. What do you think, Greg?

Greene: I think that’s right. It’s certainly how I perceive it. It’s certainly my feeling about how the presidency and the White House have been treated over the last year and a half–plus. I would also say this. Natalie Harp is a grown woman. Just like I was a grown man when I was running those accounts and when I was working at the DNC, there were times when I came under attack for things that I wrote in my personal capacity—not in a public capacity, but that were visible to the public and the press, which followed me at the time.

And there were times when people gave me grief over wordings of social media posts I made on behalf of the Democrats. There are people who today go after the woman who runs the Democrats’ official account now, as in the time when she went after Stephen Miller, rightly so, in my opinion.

So if you are holding a position of public trust—whether that’s even just public-facing, like mine at the Democratic National Committee, or if you are on the federal salary paid by the American people, like Natalie Harp—you have to be able to accept criticism and scrutiny. And the idea that she is a damsel who needs defending from the eyes of the public who pay her salary is pathetic, frankly. I would hope she gets her big-girl pants on and faces the scrutiny that is rightly coming to her, head-on.

Sargent: Very well said. Greg Greene, thanks so much for coming on, man. We really appreciate it.

Greene: I appreciate it. Thanks.

items.title: Have We Forgotten Covid’s Lessons?
items.content_text:
In June, during the first of the record heat waves to scorch Europe this summer, “the London Ambulance Service fielded over 53,000 calls, surpassing the number received when the Covid-19 pandemic was at its height in March 2020,” Bloomberg Green reported this week. And conditions inside U.K. hospitals were “far worse” than during Covid, Fiona Brennan, an anesthetist in Cardiff, Wales, told Bloomberg. It was so hot inside surgery rooms for cancer patients that basic procedures faltered, Brennan said, adding that some patients were so sweaty that she had to constantly check that intravenous drips were not “slipping out” of their bodies.

Also, as with Covid, early mortality figures dramatically understated the death tolls to come. The U.K. Health Security Agency initially estimated that 2,877 people died from heat-related ailments in May and June. France estimated 5,700 excess deaths took place between June 17 and July 2. Other analyses, benefiting from more complete data and advanced methodology, blamed the heat for as many as 20,000 deaths across Europe. And that was before the June heat wave was followed by an additional four heat waves that surely boosted the number of sick and dying.

Europe is not the only hot spot. In India, temperatures in the capital, Delhi, soared to 54 degrees Celsius (129 degrees Fahrenheit), pushing the limits of human survival, especially for the city’s poor, and again illustrating a core injustice of the climate emergency: The people who did the least to cause it are the ones who tend to suffer the most.

But despite such parallels, there are critical differences between the Covid and climate emergencies. In the opening weeks of the pandemic, scientists weren’t sure how the virus spread, or how to treat it. By contrast, science is unequivocal that today’s extreme heat waves—and the drought and fires they’ve kindled—would be “all but impossible” without human-caused global warming driven primarily by burning oil, gas, and coal. “Summer of 2026 is another step in the escalation of our world into a sort of hotter, more dangerous planet that climate scientists have been telling us about for decades,” Jeff Goodell, the author of The Heat Will Kill You First, said on CBS News.

Another difference: When Covid emerged in early 2020, much of the news media rose to the challenge, providing science-based reporting that helped both the public and policymakers make informed decisions about how to respond. Journalists also held governments to account, puncturing claims of miracle cures and explaining the value of physical distancing and getting vaccinated.

But, with notable exceptions like those cited in this article, news coverage of this summer’s extreme weather has fallen well short of the Covid standard. Two-thirds of the articles that major U.K. newspapers published about the summer’s fires did not even mention climate change, much less explain how record heat makes fires more likely and more deadly. In the U.S., the evening newscasts of ABC, CBS, and NBC between July 13 and 19 lavished airtime on the extreme weather but did not utter the words “climate change.”

The Guardian, as usual, has kept the climate connection front and center, and on August 8, it published an opinion piece by the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, who urged government leaders in Britain and around the world to treat climate change as the emergency that scientists say it is—something Khan began doing as mayor in 2018. Khan’s call for leaders to “reduce our reliance on oil and gas” did not name names, but commentators interpreted it as pressing the new British prime minister, Andy Burnham, to rule out more North Sea oil drilling, a question Burnham has studiously avoided since taking office on July 20. Meanwhile, a petition demanding that the government present a televised emergency briefing on the climate crisis has attracted 100,000 signatures, the threshold for getting it debated in Parliament, whose next session begins September 1.

Khan was only half right, however, when he opined that “the climate emergency is here, and no one can say they didn’t see it coming.” Yes, the emergency is here, and “coming faster and harder” than even scientists expected, economist Matthew Agarwala of the University of Sussex said on Britain’s Channel 4. But as Khan’s own article goes on to lament, a small but noisy chorus of climate deniers still deny that climate change is happening at all.

Khan cites Donald Trump’s dismissal of climate change as “a con job” and calls out unnamed “opposition politicians and right-wing populists” in the U.K. He does not point out that these obstructionists represent only a small fraction of public opinion. More than eight out of 10 Britons (83 percent), as well as three out of four Americans (74 percent), want their governments to take stronger climate action, according to Gallup polling that informs Covering Climate Now’s 89 Percent Project. But the deniers appear to be more numerous than they actually are, both because they have access to far-reaching megaphones and because most news coverage does not point out how wildly their claims are contradicted by science.

Again, the contrast with media coverage of Covid is striking. On April 23, 2020, as Covid’s death toll was mounting, Trump suggested at a White House press briefing that injecting disinfectant into the body might kill the virus. News outlets responded with a flurry of stories quoting incredulous experts lambasting Trump’s idea as dangerous nonsense. Trump quickly retreated, claiming that he’d been speaking sarcastically (though video of his remarks showed he was serious).

Now, as the summer of 2026 brings record heat to much of the world, as thousands die and many thousands more endure various degrees of misery, White House reporters do not even ask Trump about climate change, much less challenge his scientifically disproven assertion that it’s a hoax. In the U.K., press coverage largely ignores the climate argument against more North Sea oil drilling, instead framing Burnham’s upcoming decision as the latest battle in the culture wars.

Most journalists did better than this during Covid, and the public needs us to do better now.

This article is published as part of the global journalism collaboration Covering Climate Now.

items.title: Medicare for All Is Making a Comeback
items.content_text:
The situation is dire. Millions of people in the United States are months away from losing their health care. On January 1, dramatic changes to Medicaid outlined in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or OBBA, will take effect, impacting who is eligible for Medicaid. The new law excludes some groups completely (like most immigrants), introduces “community engagement” requirements (defined as 80 hours a month of work, volunteering, or school) for most people (apart from the elderly, children, and pregnant women), and requires renewals twice a year (as opposed to yearly). Some people have been impacted already (Nebraska implemented its changes on May 1 and began disenrolling people this month), and some will be kicked off their health care in October, when some previously qualified immigrants are made ineligible for Medicaid.

Though 92 percent of people should remain eligible for Medicaid coverage (through either a qualifying exemption or meeting the community engagement requirements), millions will still end up losing care. This is because of the substantial bureaucratic hurdles the OBBA introduces. In addition to increasing the intervals during which people must reverify their eligibility, the government has introduced an onerous process for documenting exemptions to the “community engagement” (i.e., work) requirements.

The process has become a maze of bureaucratic imposition. According to the Center for Medicaid and Medicare Services, you can get an exemption if you have a diagnosis that meets the criteria for being “medically frail.” However, the government has decided to go even further, potentially requiring attestation from a medical provider that an individual’s condition is sufficiently debilitating to keep them from working. The government cites “cancer” and “HIV/AIDS” as examples of conditions that need such a doctor’s note. A number of states have sued the federal government, arguing that this process differs from the law Congress wrote.

If just reading about this sounds confusing, that’s the point. Bureaucratic hurdles are designed with the intent to narrow the number of people who get Medicaid and therefore reduce how much the federal government spends on care. Instead, state governments will spend millions of dollars on administrative costs; data, software, consultants, and workers needed to process extra forms. When Georgia implemented work requirements for Medicaid in 2023, it cost $40 million to implement, and 80 percent of that cost was administrative. The OBBA changes will also have a profound economic cost: Some estimates suggest a loss of 1.2 million jobs and a decrease in gross domestic product by $154 billion when the law is fully implemented in 2029.

The counter to this chaos is simple—and it’s something we’re starting to hear about on the stump from Democratic candidates. As Vox’s Rachel Cohen reports, the health care reform debate has shifted in the direction of improving on the status quo and an openness to bigger ideas. And while candidates like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who Cohen notes is flexible on how the system might be improved, on the stump he keeps mentioning a more familiar idea: We could have a national health insurance program, better known as “Medicare for All.” Given the wreckage of the Trump era, Medicare for All has a lot to recommend.

In places such as Canada and the United Kingdom, you don’t worry about having to pay for lifesaving procedures, knowing that the government will pay for it. Getting procedures preapproved by an insurance bureaucrat is not part of the equation, and being buried in thousands of dollars of medical debt is not a concept that exists. These systems may not be perfect, but it is clear on key metrics that the United States does worse on health care than our industrialized counterparts. As just one example, the U.S. has worse life expectancy than most other high-income countries, yet we spend far more per capita than any other nation on health care.

The American health care system is no stranger to complexity. Even for those on private insurance, people are used to having to spend hours on the phone to get their care covered, doctors argue with insurance representatives on prior authorizations, and people have to navigate a labyrinth of numbers and lists—who is in network, what is the deductible, and what are the out-of-pocket maximums. If you buy health care on the Obamacare marketplace, it means having to decide what sort of trade-offs between coverage and cost you need to make when picking a plan. Americans hate dealing with insurance so much that one in four people will stay in a job they do not like in order to keep their commercial health insurance.

For the past few decades in the U.S., academics and politicians alike have treated Medicare for All as a “pie in the sky” idea. Despite studies showing that it would save billions of dollars and thousands of lives, this avenue has largely been unpursued, and instead, incremental steps have been taken to expand health care access. The Affordable Care Act, or ACA, was a monumental step in the right direction—among other things, it expanded Medicaid eligibility greatly.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, the federal government chose to continuously enroll people in Medicaid, keeping millions on health care (by avoiding needless bureaucracy), and Congress passed tax credits for the ACA marketplace (via the American Rescue Plan) and later extended them via the Inflation Reduction Act, bringing down the cost of monthly premiums dramatically. But in many cases, these wins turned out to be temporary. In 2023, continuous enrollment ended and millions were disenrolled from Medicaid. After Congress and the Trump administration let ACA subsidies lapse at the end of 2025, three million fewer people got their health care from the ACA marketplace.

Even though the ACA faced legal and legislative challenges, it has mostly survived. Now Medicaid is facing dramatic cuts. Medicare for All will similarly be an uphill battle, but the lesson we should garner from past experiences is that those who seek the complete privatization of health care in the United States will continue to be relentless at rolling back progress. Any attempt to expand health care or protect gains will be met with organized political resistance; so why not go for the moon? After all, polls show that Medicare for All is increasingly popular and, depending on the poll, has a majority or plurality support.

Medicare for All would not just be an easier experience for patients and doctors; it would also make dealing with a litany of American social problems a whole lot easier. Take treatment for substance use disorder, which is mostly funded through Medicaid. Currently, under the proposed “medical frailty rules,” someone who receives treatment for substance use disorder would be eligible for an exemption to the community engagement requirements, unless they have been in recovery for more than five years. Never mind the fact that recovery is a unique experience and challenging to define, this arbitrary policy could be disruptive and further complicate recovery and addiction treatment. It’s why treatment providers are so worried: having to focus on bureaucracy and paperwork to keep people covered, rather than spending time on care itself.

Contrast that with Medicare for All: A patient gets referred to treatment, the government pays for it with fewer bureaucratic steps, and there are no worries about jumping through hoops to continue to qualify for care. It would be a similar story across the health care system.

The next few years will be rough for the health care industry and patients alike. Hospitals will face enormous budgetary strains as they provide emergency care to people without insurance. Despite the best efforts of many states to keep people enrolled, millions will still likely lose care. Millions more will spend needless hours on bureaucracy and paperwork. While we may be a few years away from being able to implement a real universal health care plan, now is the time to start following the lead of El-Sayed and others to build the groundwork and start pitching it as a serious path forward. Academics, policymakers, professional societies, unions, and others should be relentless in their demand for Medicare for All.

Imagine a world where health insurance wasn’t tied to your job. Where employers didn’t have to negotiate with health insurance companies; where your monthly premium went toward taxes for an all-encompassing plan. A world where you don’t have to worry about making “too much money,” so that you lose your comprehensive health care (most people who work and receive Medicaid are in jobs that don’t provide insurance). That’s a world with Medicare for All.

Life is unaffordable for so many Americans, and managing your health can be difficult—but health care shouldn’t be a luxury that only the rich can afford. It really is that simple.

items.title: Why Democrats Must Embrace a “Mom Populist” Education Agenda
items.content_text:
Pease Elementary in downtown Austin, Texas, has sat empty since 2020. Formerly the oldest continuously operating school in Texas, Pease was shuttered by the Austin Independent School District to save money. On a steamy day this summer, the hulking structure provided an appropriate backdrop for the political campaign of Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic state representative who is challenging incumbent GOP Governor Greg Abbott.

A district plan to close the school in 2012, while Hinojosa’s son was a student there, inspired her political career, sending her first to the school board and then, four years later, to the Statehouse just a few blocks away. But Pease is also symbolic of Texas’s surprisingly fierce attachment to public education. The school dates back to 1876, the same year that the current state constitution enshrined “a system of public free schools”—a factoid that Texas advocates drop with regularity. That Pease is no longer a school matters, too. Since late 2023, at least 135 Texas public schools either have closed or are slated to close due to budget crises brought on by state funding shortfalls.

Hinojosa believes her message that Texas public schools won’t survive another four years of Abbott can galvanize voters across the political spectrum. “For Texans, public schools are crucial to our identity,” Hinojosa told me. “They’re in our state constitution, they’re the largest employers in our rural communities, they represent ‘Friday night lights.’ That they are in crisis is a big deal.”

Her decision to make public schools so central to the campaign may seem like a risky gambit. Education, after all, rarely cracks the top five when it comes to issues Texans claim to care about, far overshadowed by the economy and immigration. And according to polling, just one in five Texas voters has school-age children. The “Pissed Off Texas Mom” T-shirts are a staple of rallies for the candidate whom supporters call simply “Gina,” but in reality, the demographic may be too small to make a difference.

Hinojosa’s critique goes far beyond budget cuts and declining test scores. Schools are the centerpiece of what she argues has been an organized effort by Abbott and the GOP to rig the system against the state’s kids, especially those in working-class families like those she grew up with in Brownsville. Call it “mom populism”—an appeal that centers a full-throated rejection of school privatization and presents the GOP’s increasingly aggressive interventions into local school districts as “corruption schemes” intended to benefit big donors, especially the right-wing oilmen who hold such sway here. By systematically weakening public schools, Hinojosa argues, Abbott and his cronies are undermining the American Dream.

Beating a three-term GOP incumbent in a state like Texas remains a tall order, but there are signs that Hinojosa’s argument may just be breaking through. While Abbott, who is running for an unprecedented fourth term, comes to this fight with a massive war chest, Republicans in Texas are restive, and education is part of their discontent. The $1 billion school voucher program that Abbott muscled through the state legislature last year, after he orchestrated primary runs against rural Republicans who opposed it, remains deeply controversial among many conservatives, who view vouchers less as “education freedom” than as a state takeover of private and home schools.

Michael Ryan is one of Abbott’s defectors. A retired educator, Ryan served on the school board in Fort Worth until the state took over the district last year, installing handpicked leaders. “I’m as red a Republican as they come, but I have to do something different,” said Ryan, a three-time Trump voter. Hinojosa’s pledge to fire Abbott’s top education official on day one won him over, along with her sharp critique of school vouchers and the big money that flooded into the state on their behalf. Ryan was particularly rankled by the $10 million Abbott received from Pennsylvania billionaire investor Jeff Yass. “In the old days, a bribe meant $100 on the floor of the Capitol,” said Ryan.

Recent elections indicate that defectors like Ryan are part of a trend. This January, Democrat Taylor Rehmet, a veteran and union machinist, handily defeated a conservative activist in a special election for a state Senate seat in Tarrant County, a seat Democrats last held in 1991. Despite being far outspent by his opponent, Rehmet won by a decisive 14-point margin in a district Donald Trump carried by 17 points in 2024, alarming Republicans, not just in Texas, but across the country. “[A] swing of this magnitude is not something that can be dismissed,” chimed in Florida Governor Ron DeSantis on X. Rehmet used his background as a union leader at Lockheed Martin to win over working-class voters, but he also made public education central to his campaign, sounding many of the same themes that Hinojosa is running on now.

Affordability was the top issue for voters, but their economic concerns were often entwined with worries over the state of the local schools, said Rehmet, who grew up in a Republican household in Garland, the son of an aircraft mechanic and a beautician. “People are feeling the affordability crunch in the schools. Funding is down, the cost of living is up. You’ve got teachers paying for supplies out of their own salaries.” In a part of the state that has been ground zero for conservative school board takeovers and book bans, Rehmet also tapped into a deepening voter backlash against GOP culture-warring candidates, who have racked up a lengthening string of losses in Tarrant County.

A recent analysis of this spring’s GOP primary turnout in Texas warned that the party’s historically reliable voters were dangerously disengaged, “either sitting out this cycle or, in some cases, shifting their partisan affiliation entirely.” The phenomenon was most pronounced in suburban districts, the pollsters concluded.

That finding comes as no surprise to Hinojosa. “People know who has been in charge,” she told me, “and they want change.”


Mom Populism

Texas isn’t the only state where education has emerged as a potent issue for Democrats. As of March 2026, in the 30 state legislative races where Democrats have flipped seats since Trump returned to office, public education was often a central issue. It’s not hard to see why. As the GOP has shifted sharply in favor of private school vouchers, Democrats are increasingly running against candidates who no longer believe in public education at all, even as constituents in both parties still have kids in the local schools. Ascendant populist Democrats are also tapping into anti-billionaire fury as they campaign against vouchers. And with affordability top of mind in nearly every election these days, Democrats are effectively linking issues like school budget cuts and teacher pay to voters’ broader economic concerns.

“Republicans have no answer to affordability except for eliminating the property tax, which would devastate public schools,” said Eric Gisler, who flipped a Statehouse seat in Georgia in 2025. “That makes education a real wedge issue.”

That Democrats are running—and winning—at least in part on education may seem surprising, given the dire reporting on the state of the nation’s schools. In recent years, the headlines have been relentlessly bleak—sliding test scores in math and reading, a “learning recession,” high rates of chronic absenteeism.

The cascade of bad news has prompted loud calls from influential centrist Democrats, including possible 2028 presidential contender Rahm Emanuel, to return to the more combative education policies of the past in an effort to reverse sagging student achievement. But these Democrats are also making a political argument about the direction of their party. Bring back the high-stakes testing and tough-on-teachers rhetoric of the Obama era, goes this line of thinking, and the party can win back fickle voters. “We’re adrift, it’s killing us politically, and it’s killing our kids,” former Obama Education Secretary Arne Duncan claimed recently.

Yet as I’ve talked to Democrats who flipped seats in districts won by Trump, or who are running surprisingly competitive races in red states, a very different picture has emerged. Candidates like Taylor Rehmet are attracting independents and even former GOP voters by arguing not that the schools are failing, but that kids and communities are being failed by politicians who have abandoned public schools. “We want high standards, but we want them to be fair,” said Rehmet. “If we don’t provide enough funding, isn’t that sabotage?”

And again and again, I heard the strains of an emergent “mom populism,” from male and female candidates alike, that makes an argument for public schools as a vehicle for collective economic uplift. Notably, these Democrats are not claiming that education alone can lift kids out of poverty, or that sending more kids to college is the way to address inequality—an argument that has proved to be a political trap for the party. Instead, candidates often pair their defense of public schools as institutions that benefit working-class kids with populist calls for higher wages and more worker power. When it comes to issues like school vouchers, the influence of teachers’ unions, and college-for-all, these mom populists are departing dramatically from the prescription offered by centrist Democrats, and they’re winning as a result.


Reverse Robin Hood

When Denise Powell emerged as the winner of a hard-fought six-person Democratic primary in Nebraska’s 2nd congressional district last spring, her victory was regarded as an upset. After all, Powell triumphed over much better known candidates, including the descendant of one of the state’s political dynasties. In November, the business and nonprofit consultant will try to flip the seat being vacated by GOP veteran Don Bacon, something Democrats here have tried—and failed—to do for nearly a decade. The contest, regarded as one of the Democrats’ best chances for a pickup, is currently rated as a toss-up, but Powell is convinced that she is uniquely suited to appeal to the independents and former GOP voters she’ll need to win.

Two years ago, when opponents of school vouchers sought to put the issue before Nebraska voters, Powell crisscrossed the state to gather signatures, including in its most rural, deepest red stretches. “At a July Fourth celebration, I had a guy wearing a ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ T-shirt come up to me and ask, ‘Where do I sign?’” she said. While Powell was working on multiple ballot campaigns that summer, including one that would have expanded reproductive rights, it was her experience talking to conservative voters about vouchers that prepared her to run for Congress. “I’d walk up a dirt road to a house flying a Trump flag, but we found common ground, and it was around public education,” said Powell.

Opposition to school vouchers turns out to have been a consistent, and underappreciated, ingredient in recent special elections in which Democrats have flipped Statehouse seats in Florida, Iowa, New Hampshire, and Georgia. In North Texas, Taylor Rehmet made his objection to funding private religious schools with taxpayer money a centerpiece of his campaign. “We shouldn’t be sending public dollars to private schools with no oversight,” said Rehmet, a position that he said resonated with voters across party lines.

In a sign of just how controversial the issue is among conservatives, Rehmet’s opponent, Leigh Wambsganss, chief communications officer at a Christian nationalist cell phone company, was initially a no on Abbott’s signature education policy of vouchers, then changed her position to align with the governor—and the big donors who funded her campaign. Indeed, when the editor of a conservative news outlet asked Wambsganss’s supporters about why they thought she’d lost, they specifically mentioned her flip-flop on vouchers.

That the GOP’s hard pivot against public education has created an opening for Democrats isn’t that surprising. While school vouchers have spread wildly in recent years, particularly in red states, their track record among voters remains dismal. The Nebraska ballot initiative that Denise Powell worked on, which would have created a so-called private school scholarship program, was rejected by nearly 60 percent of voters, even as the state overwhelmingly supported the reelection of Trump. Kentucky voters rejected an attempt to amend their state constitution to allow vouchers by an even more decisive margin. Ignoring a high-profile endorsement from Trump, every single county voted against the measure, with some of the reddest counties the most emphatic in saying no to allowing public dollars to fund private religious education. That MAGA faithful would buck the boss on one of his policy priorities might seem surprising until you consider that voters have been thumbing their noses at vouchers for the past five decades. “Choice proposals have consistently lost in state after state,” concluded a trio of scholars in a postelection analysis, “often by overwhelming margins.”

At a time of populist fervor on the both the left and the right, a policy that is the pet cause of billionaires including Betsy DeVos, Trump’s much-loathed former secretary of education, and Jeff Yass, the wealthiest man in Pennsylvania, seems uniquely calibrated to arouse the ire of voters. So-called universal vouchers, which subsidize the private school tuition of even the wealthiest families, are also a remarkably efficient means of redirecting resources upward. A 2025 analysis of universal or near-universal programs in six states, including Arizona, Indiana, and North Carolina, found that vouchers “were disproportionately used by families in wealthy areas.”

Iowa, which implemented a voucher program in 2023, now spends more than $250 million to pick up the tab for students at private religious schools, the vast majority of whom never attended public schools. Catelin Drey flipped an Iowa state Senate seat with a decisive 2025 special election win, ending the Republican supermajority in that chamber and becoming its only mother of a young child. Drey made vouchers a symbol of the state’s conservative political leaders’ disregard for the struggles of ordinary Iowans, which include watching their public schools shrink and close as resources are increasingly shifted to the wealthy. “We’ve now got a voucher program with no income levels, no guidelines, and an unlimited line item in the budget,” said Drey. “Yet our public schools that serve the vast majority of kids, and do it without question, are doing it with two nickels and a stick of gum.”

The issue is also likely to help determine whether Iowans elect a Democratic governor for the first time in 16 years. On the stump, Democratic candidate Rob Sand rails against vouchers constantly, describing them as “an ideological errand-running program with no accountability paying for the wealthiest families in the state of Iowa to send their kids to the private schools they were going to send them to anyway.” His strategy seems to be paying off. Sand, elected twice as the state auditor, and currently the only Democrat holding statewide elected office in Iowa, has a slight edge over Republican Zach Lahn, previously an operative for the Koch-backed political group Americans for Prosperity. An ardent voucher proponent, Lahn helped start a private school in Wichita, Kansas, with Charles Koch’s son, Chase, before running off with the younger Koch’s wife. Lahn is running as an outsider against what he calls the “uniparty.”


Democrat vs. Democrat

Given the minuscule number of causes that still bring voters together across party lines, opposition to vouchers would seem like a logical rallying cry for Democrats, including those who seek to draw moderates back into the party fold. Instead, the issue is fueling yet another intraparty divide.

Tucked into the budget behemoth known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act was the nation’s very first federal voucher program. Starting next year, individual taxpayers will be able to donate up to $1,700 annually to so-called scholarship-granting organizations and subtract the full amount from what they owe the federal government—a uniquely generous tax credit. The nonprofits that receive the money then bundle it, after taking a cool 10 percent off the top, before redistributing it as scholarships to individual students to pay for private school tuition, tutoring, and a long list of other educational expenses.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit is as controversial as it is convoluted. Thirty U.S. senators, led by Arizona Democrat Mark Kelly, a near-certain 2028 contender, filed a bill last spring that would repeal the program. “School Vouchers Broke Arizona,” read the headline to Kelly’s excoriating op-ed, warning that his home state’s nearly $1 billion-per-year universal voucher program is a fraud-ridden budget buster that is endangering the ability of working-class kids to get a good education. “We should not take Arizona’s failed experiment national,” Kelly concluded.

But the program also has influential Democratic backers. Democrats for Education Reform, or DFER, the two-decade-old advocacy group started by New York City hedge fund managers, is at the helm of an intense lobbying effort to press Democratic governors to opt into the program. Of the 31 governors who have signed on to date, just two are Democrats. Colorado’s outgoing Governor Jared Polis opted in his state as part of a flurry of late-­office activity, including commuting the sentence of MAGA election denier Tina Peters for plotting to tamper with voting machines, then firing officials who opposed the move. New York’s Kathy Hochul, meanwhile, offered an unusually blunt justification for signing her state up: She needs Jewish votes. “Tuition relief” for students who attend religious yeshivas ranks nearly as high as support for Israel as a priority for Orthodox Jewish voters, a group that overwhelmingly backed Hochul’s GOP rival in 2022.

DFER’s sales pitch is predominantly about money. Because some portion of the funds raised can be used to benefit students who attend public schools, opting in is a “no-brainer,” as the group’s CEO, former Providence, Rhode Island, Mayor Jorge Elorza, and Arne Duncan, now a DFER senior fellow, co-wrote for The Washington Post. There’s also an attempt to present the tax credit program, which is projected to cost the U.S. Treasury nearly $26 billion in its first decade, as a vehicle for anti-Trump activism. Deprive Trump of tax dollars, goes the thinking, and he’ll have a harder time carrying out his nefarious schemes. “I would rather help kids struggling in my home state to catch up and have a chance to be successful in life, instead of sending another dollar to D.C. to fund ICE to come attack us,” argued Duncan, who is tasked with shaping the Democrats’ education policy, in a recent interview.

The U.S. Treasury, which will oversee the new tax credit program, has made it clear that governors will have no ability to impose requirements on where the money goes. Schools that discriminate against LGBTQ kids or teach PragerU content can now be funded by, well, you.

The key proponents of the program, including the American Federation for Children, the deep-pocketed lobby group started by Betsy DeVos, spin it rather differently. Moving the nation’s youngsters out of public schools and into private religious institutions that operate free of the “red tape” of civil rights protections has been a conservative movement priority for the last half-century. The program’s generous income guidelines mean that 90 percent of American students will be eligible for a voucher. Meanwhile, Treasury, which will oversee the program, has made it clear that governors will have no ability to impose requirements on where the money goes. Schools that discriminate against LGBTQ kids or teach PragerU content can now be funded by, well, you.


The Union Tussle

The Dem-on-Dem tussle over school vouchers is the latest installment of a much longer skirmish over the role of teachers’ unions within the party. DFER, after all, was founded to serve as an organized and well-funded counterweight to the unions’ influence. While the shine is off the causes the group championed during the Obama era—charter schools, merit pay, and tougher teacher evaluations yoked to student standardized test scores—the argument that Democrats need to take it to the unions has found new purchase in these days of “abundance” and combative centrism. As pundit Josh Barro put it: “Some of ‘the Groups’ are unions, and Democrats need to be better at saying no to them, too.”

It is an article of faith among centrist Democrats that voters’ low regard for the party can be explained at least in part by the Biden administration’s caving to the unions, backing away from test-based accountability and standards. Duncan has even made the case that Kamala Harris might have won in 2024 had the Democrats stuck with the education policies of his boss. The argument that Democrats prosper politically when they embrace positions that rankle teachers and their unions is also central to Rahm Emanuel’s presidential test run. “Clinton did public school choice. Obama did Race to the Top, accountability, and Common Core,” Emanuel told me, referring to the uniform math and English standards that inspired a bipartisan revolt.

Emanuel’s model for reform these days is Mississippi, whose oft-touted miracle has seen impressive academic gains, especially from elementary school students, in the country’s poorest state. “Mississippi shows the combination to the lock,” Emanuel said, describing the emphasis on phonics and strict accountability for teachers and students that has made the state an outlier in a sea of sliding test scores. But that combination also includes teachers’ unions that are relatively powerless, a product of right-to-work laws adopted in the 1950s in an effort to keep wages low and workers, especially Black workers, weak.

For Emanuel, Exhibit A of the Biden Democrats’ capitulation to teachers’ unions was pandemic school closures, what he refers to as the “original sin” of allowing politics to triumph over science. “Voters trust Democrats less than they did six years ago,” said Emanuel. Another leading centrist voice, Massachusetts Representative Jake Auchincloss, insists that Democrats need to apologize to the American people for their role in shuttering schools during Covid. “Any conversation about education needs to start with the catastrophe of the school closures,” Auchincloss told me. “We were wrong, and we won’t do it again.”

But to whom Democrats should apologize is unclear. While research has found that school districts with powerful unions stayed closed for longer, that does not seem to have translated into voter backlash. Late last year, the centrist publication The Argument set out to document the lingering damage done to the Democratic Party from its response to Covid-19. “The only problem is that our poll provided absolutely nothing to back this up,” conceded pollster Lakshya Jain. “If anything, it suggested the opposite.” The data on public opinion regarding school closures, widely understood to be Democrats’ biggest failure, Jain noted, was particularly striking. Republicans and Trump got worse marks from respondents than Biden and the Democrats. And five years after the pandemic, an outright majority of 54 percent Americans believe the shutdowns were “largely necessary” in order to prevent infections, with just 35 percent saying they were “largely unnecessary.”

This gap between rhetoric and public opinion is indicative of a larger problem underlying the centrist project of taking on teachers’ unions in hopes of luring back disaffected voters. In a review of survey data old and new, political scientist Michael Hartney finds that, in the Trump era, Democratic voters have become wildly more supportive of teachers’ unions, which they’ve come to view as “progressive bulwarks” against Trump and the GOP. The more that the unions present themselves as key actors in the progressive coalition, the more Democratic voters like them—which poses a major challenge to the case being made by Emanuel and others.

“Unions are always made out to be these big, bureaucratic institutions, but they don’t exist without members. It’s the teacher in your kid’s classroom,” said Brian Nathan, a union electrician and veteran who shocked Florida’s political establishment last spring when he flipped a state Senate seat in a reliably red part of Tampa. Nathan, whose campaign motto was “steel-toed integrity,” made teacher pay a central focus of the race, continually reminding voters that Florida now ranks dead last in how much teachers earn, and that their own kids are paying the price. “My eldest daughter had a permanent sub for an entire year,” said Nathan. “That’s the result of people fleeing the profession.”


The College Conundrum

In the waning days of a crowded Democratic primary race to represent Pennsylvania’s 7th congressional district, which includes Allentown, Ryan Crosswell, a former prosecutor for the Justice Department, suggested that his opponent, retired firefighter Bob Brooks, was a “flawed candidate” because he hadn’t gone to college. Brooks pounced. “Sorry I wasn’t lucky enough to go to college,” he pronounced on X, accusing Crosswell of “contempt” for working-class voters. Brooks would go on to win the four-person race by nearly 20 points, setting himself up for what is likely to be a fierce midterm contest against Republican Ryan Mackenzie. Should voters in the former coal and steel towns of the Lehigh Valley give him the nod, Brooks will join a select few in Congress: representatives without college degrees.

“It’s important that we run candidates who have lived real lives—it’s not just about going to college,” Brooks told me when I interviewed him after his win. Brooks’s working-class identity, beginning with his first job as a paper boy at age 10, was central to his campaign. But the flip side of his “I’m just like you” appeal to voters in a district where college-degree holders are a minority was the argument that his better-educated opponent wasn’t like them. “Going from Harvard to Harrisburg to D.C. doesn’t mean you understand what people are dealing with,” said Brooks. “And people voted that way.”

Brooks is one of a growing number of blue-collar Democrats running for office on populist platforms, ranks that include union leaders like Brian Nathan in Florida, Taylor Rehmet in Texas, and Rebecca Cooke, a waitress who grew up on a dairy farm in Wisconsin and is set to challenge incumbent Derrick Van Orden. While at least some of these candidates attended college, they’re united in their belief that college should not be the only path to economic security. The appeal of this argument isn’t hard to understand when you consider that more than 60 percent of American adults don’t have a four-year college degree.

But it also presents Democrats with a conundrum.

For decades now, Democrats have sold education, and specifically college, as the pathway to economic mobility; “what you earn depends on what you can learn,” in the parlance of Bill Clinton. By 2009, Barack Obama was warning the nation that recovering from the financial crisis would require more than just pluck. “[E]very American will need to get more than a high school diploma,” he proclaimed in his first joint address to Congress. By 2016, the percentage of young Americans with a two-year degree or higher had risen to 51 percent, a historic high. Yet even as the administration celebrated rising college-going rates, the political backlash to an economic policy that seemed to blame workers themselves for their financial difficulties was getting harder to ignore.
